AI in every phase of how we build software
Accelerate delivery • Improve quality • Reduce cost • Strengthen security & governance
The premise

We are embedding AI — Claude on Microsoft AI Foundry — into every phase of how we build software. Not to replace you. To give you a credible co-worker that drafts, summarises, generates, predicts and validates, so the human work moves to the things that need a human. Every phase. Every team. Governed by default, secure by design.
Seven phases. One operating model.
What this delivers
What this means for you
What does NOT change
• You are accountable for what you commit, deploy, send or decide. AI is a tool, not an alibi.
• Code review, security scanning, change-approval gates and customer-impact governance all stay exactly as they are.
• Customer data, secrets and production credentials never enter prompts. Use the approved tools, on managed devices, on synthetic / sanctioned data.
• If you don't know whether a use case needs Council registration, raise it as an intake — that's the lightweight way.
Where to go for more
AI-First. Cloud-Native. Secure by Design. Governed by Default.
Claude in Microsoft AI Foundry, embedded across the SDLC, delivering secure, trusted and high-impact outcomes.

sections.heading: Executive Summary
paras: SDLC 2.0 is the operating model for how the engineering function delivers software with AI embedded across every phase of the lifecycle. It does not replace the traditional Software Development Lifecycle — it augments it. Every phase from Plan through Maintain gains an AI capability, executed through Claude on Microsoft AI Foundry, governed by the existing Microsoft enterprise stack, and surfaced through the tools engineers already use.

The model is built on four design principles, summarised in the strategy graphic and reflected throughout this document. AI-First — every phase has a defined AI augmentation. Cloud-Native — runs on Azure and Microsoft AI Foundry, no parallel cloud stack. Secure by Design — inherits the organisation's identity, data and network controls; no exception path. Governed by Default — every AI interaction is logged, attributed and monitored against the AI Governance Framework v1.0.

This document is the authoritative reference for SDLC 2.0. Every team can use it to understand what AI capability is available at each phase, which tools deliver it, who is accountable, what governance applies, and what the expected outcome is. It is paired with the SDLC 2.0 Staff One-Pager (the same content distilled for broad communication) and the SDLC 2.0 section on the Intelligence Hub (the visible operating picture).

sections.heading: Headline outcomes
paras: Targets are programme-level for Year-1; per-team baselines and targets are set at squad level (see SDLC 2.0 Implementation Roadmap §10).

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Intent — Why SDLC 2.0
paras: Software is the dominant cost line of the AI & Automation programme. A 20–40% efficiency improvement on the SDLC funds every other investment we want to make.
Engineers expect AI tooling. Without a sanctioned, governed approach, individual engineers will reach for unapproved tools, leaking code and IP. The right move is to lead, not block.

The Microsoft + Foundry stack lowers the integration burden. Claude on Foundry sits inside the same Azure environment that already hosts our identity, data, network and monitoring. There is no second cloud to govern.

Quality, security and governance can improve at the same time as speed. AI-augmented review, security scanning, deployment validation and runbook generation all reduce the rate of human-error defects, not increase them.

The frontier is moving fast. Anchoring on the Foundry platform plus a defined SDLC integration pattern means we can adopt new model capabilities (Claude versions, agent patterns, evaluation tooling) without re-architecting how engineers work.

sections.heading: 2. The Framework — Seven Phases of SDLC 2.0
paras: Each traditional SDLC phase is augmented with a defined AI capability. The following table is the canonical view; deeper detail per phase follows in §2.1–§2.7.
Maturity reflects current organisational readiness, not the strength of the underlying AI capability. All seven phases will reach 'High' by end of Year-1 per the roadmap in §10.

sections.heading: 2.1 Phase 1 — Plan & Requirements — AI-Powered Discovery
paras: Traditional activity: Define objectives, gather requirements from business stakeholders, prioritise backlog, agree scope.

AI augmentation: Claude reads source material (emails, transcripts, contracts, existing docs, support tickets), distils it into structured requirements, surfaces inconsistencies and gaps, and produces a first-draft prioritised backlog for human review.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Summarise long business documents (RFPs, regulatory texts, vendor specs) into structured requirement candidates.
Extract candidate requirements from email threads, Teams chat archives, meeting transcripts.
Cluster duplicate or overlapping requirements across multiple inputs.
Identify gaps, ambiguities, missing acceptance criteria, conflicting constraints.
Prioritise candidate items against business outcomes using configurable scoring (value vs. effort, regulatory weight, customer impact).

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: Business Analyst owns; Product Manager and Tech Lead validate. AI-drafted requirements are never committed to a sprint without explicit human review and product sign-off.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: Use cases are registered in the AI Use-Case Register (Framework §6) where AI materially shapes a backlog at scale.
Source material containing personal data follows the data-handling rules in the AUP §5 and §7.

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: 30–50% reduction in time from raw input to a structured first-draft backlog.
Higher requirement coverage on long source documents — fewer surprises in build.
Documented audit trail of which input drove which requirement (traceability).

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: Hallucinated requirements that look plausible but were not in the source — mitigated by mandatory citation back to source paragraph.
Bias in prioritisation if scoring model is opaque — mitigated by published scoring criteria and human override on prioritisation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Phase 2 — Design — AI-Assisted Design
paras: Traditional activity: Create solution architecture, data models, API specifications, UI/UX designs based on agreed requirements.

AI augmentation: Claude generates architecture options for a given problem, drafts data models and API contracts from requirements, produces UI/UX wireframes and prototypes, and explains trade-offs between options.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Generate two or three candidate architectures for a given requirement set, with trade-off analysis.
Draft data model (ER diagrams, schema, table-level designs) from a written feature description.
Draft API contracts (OpenAPI / Swagger) from user stories.
Generate UI/UX wireframes and low-fidelity prototypes from a description.
Compare a proposed design against existing architectural patterns and standards in the organisation; flag deviations.

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: Solution Architect owns; Tech Lead and Security Architect validate. AI-generated designs are reviewed in the standard architecture-review forum before commitment.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: Designs that introduce a new data class, integration or model dependency follow the AI Use-Case intake (Framework §6).
Design reviews include explicit consideration of AI-output risks (hallucinated APIs, fictional libraries, deprecated patterns).

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: Faster generation of design alternatives — architects evaluate options instead of starting from blank.
More consistent adherence to standards — AI flags deviations during drafting, not at review.
Better-quality first-draft API contracts and schemas, reducing rework in build.

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: AI-fabricated APIs or libraries that don't exist — mitigated by mandatory architecture-review cross-check.
Architectures that look plausible but ignore non-functional constraints (compliance, latency) — mitigated by explicit constraint prompting and Security Architect review.

sections.heading: 2.3 Phase 3 — Development — AI-Augmented Development
paras: Traditional activity: Write code, integrate components, follow coding standards, write unit tests, raise PRs.

AI augmentation: Engineers code with AI coding assistants in their IDEs. Claude generates code, completes lines, refactors, explains unfamiliar code, and converts requirements directly into testable implementations.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Inline code completion (single line, multi-line, function-level).
Generate functions, classes, modules, APIs from natural-language description or requirement.
Auto-complete repetitive code (boilerplate, configuration, schema migrations).
Refactor — rename, extract, simplify, modernise legacy patterns.
Explain unfamiliar or legacy code; translate between languages or framework versions.
Generate unit tests alongside the code they cover.

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: Engineer is accountable for what they commit. Tech Lead reviews. Security review for sensitive paths. Branch protection enforces both human reviewer and GHAS pre-merge checks regardless of who or what wrote the code.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: AI Acceptable Use Policy v1.0 §8 binds developer behaviour. Vendor SOW Addendum §3 binds vendor staff equivalently.
Code & IP controls (Control Register F.01–F.05) enforced — copyright filter on, secret scanning on, no production data in prompts.

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: 10–25% throughput uplift per engineer at squad level after baseline period.
Lower defect introduction rate when AI suggestions go through the standard review and security pipeline.
Better unit-test coverage — AI lowers the friction of writing tests.

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: Engineers accepting AI suggestions without reading them — mitigated by training, review process, and metrics on suggestion-acceptance vs. defect rate.
Secret leakage in prompts — mitigated by GHAS push protection, Dev Box isolation, AUP enforcement.
Subtle defects that pass review (AI generates plausible-but-wrong code) — mitigated by test coverage requirements and security scanning.

sections.heading: 2.4 Phase 4 — Testing — AI-Enhanced Testing
paras: Traditional activity: Test functionality, performance, security and usability against acceptance criteria.
AI augmentation: Claude generates test cases from user stories, creates test data and mocks, drafts automation scripts, and summarises test runs in human-readable form.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Generate functional test cases from user stories, with positive, negative and edge-case coverage.
Generate test data (synthetic, schema-conformant) and mock services for integration testing.
Convert manual test cases to automated scripts (Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, REST-assured).
Generate performance and load-test scenarios.
Summarise test runs — what passed, what failed, what changed in failure profile, suggested next steps.

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: QA Lead owns; Engineer validates. AI-generated tests are reviewed for meaningfulness — coverage padding does not pass review.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: Test data uses synthetic or pseudonymised content only (AUP §5.3 prohibits production data in prompts).
Generated test scripts go through the same code-review process as feature code.

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: Coverage uplift on legacy systems where tests were manual or absent.
Faster turnaround on automation backlog — AI drafts, humans validate.
Earlier defect detection — better tests, run more often.

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: False-positive coverage — tests that exercise paths but do not assert meaningfully — mitigated by mutation testing thresholds and reviewer guidance.
Brittle AI-generated automation scripts — mitigated by reviewer ownership and self-healing-test pattern adoption.

sections.heading: 2.5 Phase 5 — Deployment — AI-Assisted Deployment
paras: Traditional activity: Release to staging and production, manage configuration changes, run database migrations, communicate to stakeholders.
AI augmentation: Claude generates and validates deployment scripts and IaC templates, predicts deployment risk based on the change set, and drafts release notes from commit history.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Generate deployment scripts (Bicep, Terraform, ARM templates, Helm charts, GitHub Actions / Azure Pipelines workflows).
Validate configuration files and IaC templates against organisational standards and policies.
Predict deployment risk — based on diff size, files touched, recent change-failure history, dependencies — with traffic-light recommendation.
Auto-generate release notes from PRs and commits, in customer-facing or internal style.
Draft rollback plans aligned to the deployment plan.

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: DevOps Engineer owns; Release Manager validates. Production deployments require human approval at the gate regardless of AI risk score.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: Deployment scripts that touch production environments are reviewed under the standard change-management process.
AI risk-prediction is an input to the change-approval decision, not a substitute for it.

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: Fewer failed deployments via AI-assisted IaC validation pre-merge.
More consistent and complete release notes — both customer-facing and internal.
Faster recovery — clearer pre-written rollback plans.

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: Over-trust in AI risk predictions — mitigated by the gate requirement and tracking AI prediction accuracy over time.
AI-generated IaC introducing security misconfiguration — mitigated by Defender for Cloud policy checks and Azure Policy enforcement.

sections.heading: 2.6 Phase 6 — Operations & Monitoring — AI for Operations
paras: Traditional activity: Monitor systems, ingest logs, respond to incidents, manage performance, capacity and alerts.
AI augmentation: Claude assists Site Reliability Engineering with anomaly detection, alert correlation, log summarisation, root-cause analysis and runbook generation.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Anomaly detection on logs and metrics; alert correlation across services to reduce noise.
Log summarisation — distil thousands of lines into the relevant story for the on-call engineer.
Root-cause analysis — given an incident, propose probable causes with evidence and prior-incident references.
Predict incidents and capacity needs from telemetry trends.
Auto-generate runbooks for recurring patterns; refine existing runbooks from incident outcomes.

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: Site Reliability Engineering owns; SOC validates. Customer-impact incidents require human incident commander; AI assists, never adjudicates.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: Operations AI use cases follow the standard intake; Tier 1 (customer-impact decisioning) requires Council approval.
Sentinel ingests AI signals as detection inputs (Control Register D.02); SOC operates per the AI Monitoring & Incident Playbook.

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: Faster mean-time-to-resolve (MTTR) on incidents through better summaries and earlier root-cause hypotheses.
Reduction in alert fatigue via correlation.
Higher coverage of runbooks for recurring patterns.

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: AI summaries that misrepresent the underlying logs — mitigated by always linking to source events.
Over-reliance on AI root-cause hypotheses — mitigated by treating AI as one input alongside engineer judgement.

sections.heading: 2.7 Phase 7 — Maintenance & Evolution — AI for Evolution
paras: Traditional activity: Fix defects, enhance features, refactor, improve user experience, evolve the product continuously.
AI augmentation: Claude analyses user feedback, support tickets and telemetry to suggest improvements; recommends refactors; performs impact analysis on proposed changes.

sections.heading: Capabilities
paras: Cluster and analyse support tickets, NPS comments, app-store reviews to identify themes.
Suggest specific feature improvements grounded in clustered user evidence.
Recommend code refactors — identify hotspots, complexity, duplication.
Impact analysis for a proposed change — affected callers, downstream services, risk.
Compare current state to industry / peer patterns and suggest modernisation candidates.

sections.heading: Roles & responsibility
paras: Product Manager owns customer-feedback synthesis; Tech Lead owns code-evolution suggestions. Refactoring goes through standard PR review.

sections.heading: Governance touchpoints
paras: Customer feedback corpora may contain personal data — handle per AUP §5 and DPO guidance.
Refactor suggestions follow standard change management — AI does not refactor production code unattended.

sections.heading: Expected outcomes
paras: Better-targeted feature investment — informed by clustered user evidence rather than loudest voice.
Lower technical-debt accrual — refactor opportunities surfaced systematically.
Fewer surprise regressions — impact analysis catches downstream effects pre-merge.

sections.heading: Risks specific to this phase
paras: Bias in feedback synthesis (e.g. only English voices over-represented) — mitigated by sampling design and cross-language analysis.
Refactors that look correct but break tacit behaviours — mitigated by mandatory test coverage and impact analysis.

sections.heading: 3. Enterprise AI Platform — Microsoft AI Foundry
paras: All AI capability across SDLC 2.0 is delivered through Microsoft Azure AI Foundry. Foundry is the enterprise-grade hosting, governance and orchestration platform for AI models, including Claude. There is no shadow AI platform; there is no parallel cloud; everything inherits the existing Azure security, identity and policy posture.

sections.heading: 3.2 Why Foundry, why Claude
paras: Foundry is part of our existing Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC) — no separate procurement event is required for the platform or the Claude model consumption.
Claude on Foundry runs inside our Azure tenant. Customer data is not used to train foundation models — contractual commitment confirmed annually with the provider (Control Register B.04).

Claude's model strengths (long-context reasoning, code, tool use) align directly with the SDLC use cases. Sonnet for default coding and analysis; Haiku for fast triage; Opus for complex reasoning, with hard spend cap.
Microsoft owns the platform commercials, security posture and operational reliability. We own the use cases, the data and the governance.

sections.heading: 4. Security, Governance & Compliance
paras: SDLC 2.0 inherits the existing AI control set — there is no separate AI security regime. The same Acceptable Use Policy, Control Register, Monitoring & Incident Playbook, Vendor DDQ, Council Charter and Use-Case Intake apply.
Microsoft contractual position: 'Your data is your data. Microsoft does not use your data to train foundation models.' Verified annually per Control Register B.04.

sections.heading: 5. Enabling Capabilities
paras: The following enabling capabilities turn SDLC 2.0 from concept into a practice every team uses every day.

sections.heading: 6. How It Works — End-to-End Flow
paras: From the perspective of an engineer or analyst using AI in their daily work:
Step 1 — Ask. The user (engineer, BA, QA, ops, PM) asks a question or defines a task — in their IDE, in Teams, in Copilot Studio, or in a custom Foundry-hosted application.
Step 2 — Understand. Claude on Foundry receives the request inside our Azure tenant. Identity is the user's Entra ID. Context is the data they are authorised to access.

Step 3 — Retrieve. The model accesses authorised enterprise data (RAG), tools (APIs, connectors) and integrations on the user's behalf — only what the user can see, only what the use case is approved for.
Step 4 — Generate. The model produces a response, recommendation or artefact (text, code, query, design, summary).
Step 5 — Review. The user reviews, refines and validates the output — accountability stays with the user. AI does not commit, deploy, send, or decide unattended.
Step 6 — Integrate. The validated output flows into the SDLC workflow — a PR, a test plan, a release note, a ticket, a runbook.
Step 7 — Learn. Telemetry on the interaction (acceptance, edits, downstream outcome) is captured and feeds back into prompt improvement, model selection and capability development.

sections.heading: 8. Outcomes & Metrics — What We Measure
paras: Measurement is per squad, baselined before AI adoption, and rolled up to the programme. The programme-level targets are the ones in the Executive Summary; the per-phase contributors are below.

sections.heading: 9. Roles & Responsibilities — RACI by Phase
paras: Cross-phase accountability for the SDLC 2.0 operating model itself sits with the Head of AI & Automation (AI capability) and the Head of Software Engineering (SDLC operations) jointly.

sections.heading: 10. Implementation Roadmap
paras: Rollout follows three waves over Year-1, prioritising the phases with highest immediate productivity uplift (Development, Testing, Operations) and lowest organisational change cost. Plan and Maintain follow once the dev-loop wins are evidenced.

sections.heading: 10.1 Per-wave gates
paras: Each wave has a written go / no-go at the end. Without measurable productivity uplift on the previous wave (squad-level baselines), the next wave is paused for diagnosis.
Wave 1 (Dev + Test + Ops) is the load-bearing wave — if it doesn't show 10–15% throughput uplift on pilot squads by month 3, the rest of the rollout is reconsidered.

Binding rules for all employees, contractors and third parties using AI on behalf of the organisation

sections.heading: Read This First
paras: This policy is binding. Every person who uses an AI tool on behalf of the organisation is responsible for following it. The full policy is below; the five rules that matter most are:
RULE 1 — You are accountable for anything you produce, send, commit or decide using AI. Treat every AI output as a draft.

RULE 2 — Do not paste customer data, employee personal data, financial records, source code containing secrets, or anything labelled Confidential or Restricted into any AI tool that is not on the approved list in §6.
RULE 3 — Use only the tools on the approved list in §6, signed in with your work account, on a managed device. Personal AI accounts must never receive company data.
RULE 4 — If AI helps you produce a customer-facing decision, document, or commitment, a human (you) signs off. AI does not approve credit, deny a claim, or commit the bank.
RULE 5 — Report incidents fast. If an AI tool surfaces something you should not have seen, makes up a fact you almost used, or behaves oddly, report it within 24 hours via the channels in §10.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose and Scope
paras: This Acceptable Use Policy (the 'Policy') sets the rules for using artificial intelligence (AI) tools on behalf of the organisation. It exists to protect customers, employees and the organisation from foreseeable harms — leakage of confidential information, biased or unsafe outputs, regulatory breach, and reputational damage — while still letting people get the productivity benefit of AI.

This Policy is a binding workplace policy. It is referenced in your contract of employment and the standard contractor terms. It works alongside the AI Governance Framework v1.0 (which sets policy and accountability at organisational level), the Information Security Policy, the Data Protection Policy, and applicable local data-protection laws (POPIA, NDPA, KDPA and equivalents).

sections.heading: 1.1 Who this applies to
paras: All permanent employees, fixed-term staff, contractors, consultants, interns and seconded personnel.
Any third party using AI tools on the organisation's data, accounts or systems.
Anyone building AI-enabled software or workflows for the organisation, even on behalf of a partner.

sections.heading: 1.2 What this applies to
paras: All approved generative AI assistants in §6 (M365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot Enterprise, Claude Code on Azure AI Foundry, agents built on Copilot Studio, agents built directly on Foundry).
Use of foundation models or AI APIs in any custom application, even internal.
Use of AI features inside other approved SaaS tools where company data is processed.
Use of any AI tool — approved or not — when company data, accounts or devices are involved.

sections.heading: 3. Your Accountability
paras: AI is a tool. Accountability stays with the person, not the tool. You may not point to an AI output as the reason a mistake happened.
You are responsible for the accuracy, fairness, legality and appropriateness of anything you produce, send, commit, post, decide or communicate using AI.
You are responsible for verifying AI output before relying on it. If you cite a fact, check the source. If you commit code, you have read it. If you send an email, you have re-read it.
You are responsible for following this Policy even when it is inconvenient. If a deadline tempts you to bypass a rule, the answer is escalate, not bypass.

sections.heading: 5.1 You may
paras: Use approved AI tools on company-managed devices, signed in with your work Entra ID account.
Use approved AI tools on Internal-classified data within the limits of your role and the data-handling rules of the system.
Ask AI to draft, summarise, translate, brainstorm, code, search and explain — provided you remain accountable for the output.
Use AI to learn — to understand a concept, an error message, a piece of code, a document, a regulation.
Raise an intake (Framework §6) if you want to use AI in a way this Policy does not currently cover.

sections.heading: 5.2 You must
paras: Sign in with your work account on company-managed devices, with MFA.
Apply or respect existing sensitivity labels (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) on any document AI consumes or produces.
Verify AI output before relying on it materially.
Keep humans in the loop on any decision that affects a customer, employee or counterparty.
Report any AI incident or near-miss within 24 hours via the channels in §10.
Complete the Acceptable Use Policy attestation on joining and at least annually.

sections.heading: 5.3 You must not
paras: Paste Confidential or Restricted data into any AI tool not on the approved list in §6.
Use a personal AI account (your own ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.) to process any company data, even Internal-classified data.
Use AI to make a Material Decision without a human (you) signing off.
Use AI to generate content that misleads about its origin (e.g. impersonating a named individual; passing AI text off as a customer's words).
Use AI to circumvent a control — for example, asking a model to produce a credential, exfiltrate data, or bypass a security policy.
Bypass the AI use-case intake (Framework §6) for any new use you build or commission.
Disable, work around or hide from monitoring controls (audit logs, Sentinel, Purview, GitHub Advanced Security).

sections.heading: 6. Approved Tools
paras: Only these tools are approved for use with company data. Other AI tools require a use-case intake (Framework §6) and Council approval before use.
Restricted data (e.g. cardholder data, customer ID numbers in clear, credentials) is not permitted in any AI tool except via a Council-approved Tier 1 use case with explicit data-protection sign-off.

sections.heading: 7. Rules for M365 Copilot Users
paras: These rules apply to everyone — M365 Copilot is the AI tool you encounter most often.

sections.heading: 7.1 You may
paras: Use Copilot to summarise, draft, search and reason over content you can already access in the tenant.
Use Copilot in Word, Outlook, Teams, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote and Loop on managed devices.
Pin Copilot Pages to a Team for collaborative drafting on Internal content.

sections.heading: 7.2 You must
paras: Apply or respect Purview sensitivity labels — labels propagate to Copilot outputs.
Treat anything Copilot retrieves from a SharePoint site you did not realise you had access to as a potential oversharing incident — report it within 24 hours.
Verify any factual claim, citation, name, number, quote or policy reference before sending or publishing.
Re-read any draft before sending it externally.

sections.heading: 7.3 You must not
paras: Use Copilot to draft customer commitments (rates, conditions, approvals) without your own review and the standard approval pathway.
Use Copilot to anonymise data and then send it externally without DPO confirmation that anonymisation is sufficient.
Disable or attempt to bypass sensitivity labels on output documents.
Use Copilot on personal devices or with personal accounts.

sections.heading: 8. Rules for Developers Using AI Coding Assistants
paras: In addition to the General Rules in §5, these apply to every engineer using GitHub Copilot Enterprise, Claude Code on Foundry, or any other AI coding assistant approved on the list in §6.

sections.heading: 8.1 You may
paras: Use approved AI coding assistants on approved repositories, signed in with your work GitHub identity.
Accept AI suggestions you have read and understood; reshape suggestions before committing.
Use AI to write tests, refactor, explain code, suggest fixes, draft commit messages and PR descriptions.

sections.heading: 8.2 You must
paras: Read every suggestion before accepting it. AI-authored code is your code once you commit.
Run the standard pre-merge checks: GitHub Advanced Security (CodeQL, secret scanning, dependency review), unit tests, and Copilot Code Review where configured.
Resolve any high-severity Copilot Autofix recommendation before merge.
Treat AI-generated code that comes with a copyright filter warning as a stop signal — re-prompt or write the code yourself.
Use the standard PR review process with a human reviewer for any non-trivial change.

sections.heading: 8.3 You must not
paras: Paste customer data, production secrets, .env files, credentials, private keys, certificates or PII into prompts or test data, even temporarily.
Disable secret scanning, dependency review or branch protection rules to make a Copilot-suggested change merge faster.
Use AI suggestions in security-critical code paths (authn, authz, crypto, payment routing) without senior review and an additional security check.
Use a personal Copilot or other AI coding tool on company code or company devices.
Use AI to evade code review obligations or to merge changes that would otherwise need a second pair of eyes.

sections.heading: 9. Rules for Citizen Developers and Builders
paras: This section applies if you build agents, copilots or workflows — whether on Microsoft Copilot Studio, Power Platform or directly on Foundry.

sections.heading: 9.1 You may
paras: Build agents in approved low-code or developer environments, on Internal content.
Use approved foundation models from the Framework §7 list.
Publish agents to your team after registering the use case (Framework §6) and obtaining the appropriate approval.

sections.heading: 9.2 You must
paras: Register every agent or copilot in the AI use-case register before publishing it beyond yourself.
Use Purview-classified data sources only; do not connect agents to unclassified sources.
Apply DLP policies on the connectors your agent uses (Power Platform DLP / Copilot Studio DLP).
Provide a clear in-app disclosure that users are interacting with AI, and route to a human escalation path.
Decommission agents that no longer have an owner or a measured value.

sections.heading: 9.3 You must not
paras: Publish an agent to anyone outside yourself before registration and Council approval (or Chair-approved fast-track for Tier 3).
Connect a low-code agent to production financial, customer or HR systems without intake approval.
Build agents that make Material Decisions or commit the organisation.
Use customer data in test or development environments.

sections.heading: 10. Reporting AI Incidents
paras: If something happens that should not happen — fast or near-miss — report it. Reporting in good faith is protected; not reporting is the breach.

sections.heading: 10.1 What to report
paras: AI surfaced content you did not realise you had access to (oversharing).
AI produced a fabricated fact, citation, calculation or attribution that you almost used or did use.
AI output that appears biased, harmful, defamatory or unlawful.
Sensitive data ended up in a prompt or response.
Suspected misuse of AI by another person — internal or external.
A new AI tool being used without registration; a workaround being used to bypass an AI control.

sections.heading: 10.2 How to report
paras: Reporting is not blame. The AI Council reviews incidents to improve controls, not to punish reporters acting in good faith.

sections.heading: 11. Consequences of Breach
paras: Breaches of this Policy are managed under the standard disciplinary procedure, calibrated to severity:

sections.heading: 12. Review and Changes
paras: This Policy is reviewed at least annually by the AI Council and Head of AI & Automation.
Material changes are communicated to all staff and require fresh attestation within 30 days.
Minor changes are communicated via the intranet AI hub and noted in the change log.
The current version of this Policy is the version on the Information Security Policy library; printouts and downloads may be out of date.

sections.heading: 13. Attestation
paras: By signing this Policy (or by completing the digital attestation in the HR system), you confirm that you:
Have read and understood this AI Acceptable Use Policy.
Will follow it in your day-to-day work.
Will report any incident or near-miss within the SLAs in §10.
Understand that breaches may result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.

PART A — CHARTER

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
paras: The AI Council is the cross-functional governance forum accountable for how artificial intelligence is built, procured, deployed, operated and retired across the organisation. It exists to make AI decisions safer, faster and more defensible than any single function could on its own.

This Charter establishes the Council's terms of reference. It is the operating document of the Council and is binding on all members. It sits alongside the AI Governance Framework v1.0 (which sets the policy the Council enforces), the AI Acceptable Use Policy v1.0 (which binds individual users), the AI Control Register v1.0 (which inventories the controls the Council oversees), and the AI Monitoring & Incident Playbook v1.0 (which the Council reviews after incidents).

sections.heading: 2. Authority
paras: The Council derives its authority from the Executive Committee (ExCo), which has delegated AI governance to the Head of AI & Automation. The Council's decisions on matters within its scope are binding on the organisation, subject to the escalation paths in §11.

sections.heading: 2.1 The Council may
paras: Approve, reject, defer or condition any AI use case classified Tier 2 (limited risk) under the AI Governance Framework §5.
Recommend, with mandatory ExCo confirmation, any AI use case classified Tier 1 (high risk).
Confirm Tier 3 (minimal risk) registrations approved on Chair-delegated authority.
Add, change or remove items on the Approved Models / Approved Tools list (Framework §7).
Commission red-team exercises, independent reviews and external assurance work.
Require remediation of weak controls, with binding timelines.
Suspend or pause an AI system on safety, regulatory or material incident grounds, with immediate effect.
Update the Council's standing rules of procedure within this Charter, by majority vote.

sections.heading: 2.2 The Council may not
paras: Approve any Tier 4 (prohibited) use case — these require Executive Committee approval with documented mitigations.

Override decisions reserved to the Board, the Board Risk Committee, the Audit & Risk Committee, the CRO under the Risk Management Framework, the DPO under data-protection law, or the GC on legal matters.
Amend this Charter — amendments require ExCo approval (see §15).

sections.heading: 3. Scope
paras: All AI systems in use, in build, in pilot or under proposal across the organisation.
Vendor SaaS where AI is a material feature touching the organisation's data or customers.
AI-related policies, controls, training and assurance activity.
AI incidents, near-misses and lessons learned.
AI investment decisions within the budget envelope approved by ExCo and the Board.

sections.heading: 4.2 Rotating voting members
paras: One business-unit leader per use case under review (e.g. Head of Retail, Head of Operations, Head of Customer Experience).
Rotation is for the duration of the use case being considered; rotating members vote on that use case but do not count toward general quorum.

sections.heading: 4.3 Standing non-voting attendees
paras: Council Secretary (AI & Automation Programme Manager) — runs minutes, action log and decision log.
Internal Audit observer (rotation by quarter) — silent attendee for assurance line-of-sight.
Microsoft Customer Success representative — by invitation, on platform / tooling agenda items.

sections.heading: 4.4 Member responsibilities
paras: Read the pre-read pack at least 48 hours before the meeting.
Attend in person or via Teams; no proxy voting except for a permanent named deputy listed in §4.5.
Declare conflicts of interest at the start of any item where they exist (see §10).
Make decisions in the interests of the organisation as a whole, not the function they represent.
Treat Council pre-reads, deliberations and unpublished decisions as confidential.
Champion approved decisions back to their function and act on actions assigned.

sections.heading: 4.5 Permanent deputies
paras: Each permanent voting member nominates one named deputy in writing to the Council Secretary. The deputy may attend and vote when the principal cannot. A deputy without prior nomination has observer status only.

sections.heading: 6.1 Standing meetings
paras: Monthly standing meeting — 90 minutes — second Tuesday of each month, 10:00 local time.
Standing agenda: approvals, portfolio review, incident log, regulatory horizon scan, control health, policy change requests, AOB.
Quarterly extended session — 120 minutes — replaces a monthly when convened; deeper review of strategy and external posture.

sections.heading: 6.2 Emergency sessions
paras: Convened by Chair within 48 hours of any P1 / P2 AI incident or any Tier 4 detection.
Convened on request of the CISO, CRO or DPO with stated cause.
Emergency-session quorum is reduced to four permanent members, with at least one of CISO / DPO and at least one of CRO / risk delegate.

sections.heading: 6.3 Engagement with other forums
paras: Quarterly Board Risk Committee deep-review — written pack tabled by Chair and CISO.
Monthly summary to ExCo — written; standing agenda slot for material items.
Bi-annual review session with Internal Audit — full Council; covers control posture and audit findings.

sections.heading: 8. Subcommittees and Working Groups
paras: The Council may establish subcommittees and working groups by majority vote, with written terms of reference, named lead, named members, decision rights and end-date. Subcommittees report back at the next standing meeting.
Standing subcommittees envisaged at Year-1: Model Risk Working Group (for Tier 1 readiness); Citizen Developer Working Group (Copilot Studio governance); Vendor & Third-Party Working Group.
Working groups can take no decision the Council itself could not take; they cannot bypass quorum or voting thresholds.

sections.heading: 9. Secretariat
paras: The Council Secretary is the AI & Automation Programme Manager. The Secretary attends every meeting, has no vote, and is responsible for the operational integrity of Council records.
Maintains the Council calendar and circulates the agenda 5 working days before each meeting.
Collects, formats and circulates the pre-read pack 48 hours before each meeting.
Records minutes, the action log, the risk log and the decision log (see Part B).
Distributes minutes within 3 working days of the meeting; minutes are confirmed at the next meeting.
Maintains the membership register (principals, deputies, attendees).
Maintains the Council artefact library on SharePoint (charter, framework, register, playbook, all decision packs).
Tracks open actions to closure and reports overdue items at each meeting.

sections.heading: 10. Conflicts of Interest
paras: Members declare any actual, potential or perceived conflict in writing on appointment, and on each agenda item where one exists.
A conflicted member does not vote on the affected item, does not count toward quorum on that item, and may be asked to leave the room for that item at the Chair's discretion.
All declarations are recorded in the minutes.
The standing register of declared interests is maintained by the Secretary and reviewed quarterly.

sections.heading: 11. Escalation
paras: Matters the Council cannot resolve within two consecutive meetings are escalated to ExCo with a written recommendation.
Any matter with material regulatory exposure is escalated to the Board Risk Committee at the next available session, with interim notification by Chair.
Disagreement between the Chair and any of CISO / CRO / DPO / GC on a Tier 1 or Tier 2 matter is automatically escalated to ExCo with both positions documented.
Members may request an item be escalated; the request, the basis and the outcome are recorded.

sections.heading: 12. Confidentiality
paras: Pre-reads, deliberations, in-flight decisions and unpublished minutes are confidential to the Council.
Members may share Council outputs with their immediate function for execution, on a need-to-know basis.
Decisions of public or material interest are communicated through the agreed comms channel (Chair, CIO/CTO or CEO as appropriate), not by individual members.
Records subject to legal privilege are marked accordingly and held by the General Counsel.

sections.heading: 13. Records and Retention
paras: All retention is per the Records Management Policy; AI Council records may be discoverable in regulatory or litigation contexts and are managed accordingly.

sections.heading: 14. Performance Review of the Council
paras: Annual self-assessment by all members against this Charter; results discussed at the next quarterly extended session.
Annual external or independent review every two years (Internal Audit alternating with external).
Public-style ExCo update once a year on Council effectiveness.

sections.heading: 15. Amendment of the Charter
paras: Any member may propose amendments in writing to the Chair.
Material amendments require Council recommendation by majority and ExCo approval.
Minor amendments (clarifications, contact details, references to other documents) may be approved by Chair and recorded at the next meeting.
Charter is reviewed at least annually.
PART B — DECISION LOG TEMPLATE

sections.heading: B.1 Purpose and Discipline
paras: Every decision the Council takes is recorded in the Decision Log. The Log exists so that — months or years later — an auditor, regulator, new Council member, or affected business can answer four questions: what was decided, what was the reasoning, what conditions applied, and is it still valid.

The Log is maintained by the Secretary as a SharePoint list, with each entry exportable to PDF for audit packs. Entries are not edited after closure of the meeting; corrections are made by issuing a superseding entry and noting the link.

sections.heading: B.3 Worked Examples
paras: Three illustrative decisions showing how the template is filled in. Use these as the reference style for new entries.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose and Scope
paras: This framework sets out how artificial intelligence (AI) is built, procured, deployed, operated and retired across the organisation. It exists to let the business capture the productivity and customer-experience value of AI while meeting the obligations we owe to regulators, customers, employees and shareholders.

The framework is binding on all permanent employees, fixed-term staff, contractors, consultants and third parties who build or use AI systems on behalf of the organisation, regardless of whether those systems are built in-house, bought from a vendor, or consumed as a service.

sections.heading: 1.1 In scope
paras: Generative AI assistants, whether general-purpose (for example M365 Copilot, already deployed enterprise-wide) or purpose-built (GitHub Copilot Enterprise, Claude Code on Microsoft Foundry).
Custom AI agents and copilots built on Microsoft Copilot Studio or directly on Azure AI Foundry.
Predictive and decisioning models used in credit, fraud, AML, marketing, operations and customer service.
Any third-party SaaS product where AI is a material feature touching our data or our customers.
Experimental / research AI work including notebooks and proofs of concept that touch production or customer data.

sections.heading: 1.2 Out of scope
paras: Deterministic rule engines with no learned component (governed under existing change management).
Personal-productivity AI use where company data is NOT processed (covered by the Acceptable Use Policy in §10).

sections.heading: 2. Principles
paras: Every AI system in scope will be designed, delivered and operated in line with the following principles. They are intentionally brief — detail lives in the process sections.

sections.heading: 3. Definitions
paras: The following definitions apply throughout this framework. Where a term is not defined here, the definition from ISO/IEC 22989 (AI concepts and terminology) is used.

sections.heading: 4. AI Council
paras: The AI Council is the accountable forum for AI governance across the organisation. It is chaired by the Head of AI & Automation and meets monthly, with emergency sessions convened on material incidents.

sections.heading: 4.1 Membership
paras: Chair: Head of AI & Automation (permanent)
CIO or CTO delegate (permanent)
CISO or nominated deputy (permanent)
Chief Risk Officer or Head of Operational Risk (permanent)
Data Protection Officer (permanent)
General Counsel or nominated legal lead (permanent)
Head of Engineering (permanent)
Head of Data / Analytics (permanent)
Rotating business leader (per use case)
Secretary (AI & Automation programme manager, non-voting)

sections.heading: 4.2 Decision rights and quorum
paras: Quorum: five permanent members, including either CISO or DPO, and either the CRO or a risk delegate.
Approvals of high-risk (Tier 1) use cases require unanimous vote of permanent members present.
Approvals of Tier 2 use cases require a simple majority.
Tier 3 use cases are pre-approved subject to registration and meeting control baselines (fast-track).
Tier 4 use cases (prohibited) cannot be approved at Council level; any exception requires Executive Committee sign-off.

sections.heading: 4.3 Cadence and outputs
paras: Monthly standing meeting (90 minutes) covering: new use-case approvals, portfolio review, incident log, regulatory horizon scan, policy change requests.
Quarterly deep-review session with Board Risk Committee (60 minutes) covering portfolio posture and material changes.
Ad-hoc sessions convened within 48 hours for any material AI incident.
Outputs: approvals register, minutes, action log, decision log — all retained in the AI use-case register.

sections.heading: 4.4 Escalation
paras: Matters the Council cannot resolve within two meetings are escalated to the Executive Committee with a recommendation. Matters with enterprise-level regulatory exposure are escalated to the Board Risk Committee.

sections.heading: 5. Risk Tiering
paras: Every AI system is classified into one of four tiers. The tier sets the depth of approval, validation and monitoring required. Classification is proposed by the model owner, reviewed by the AI & Automation function, and confirmed by the AI Council.

sections.heading: 6. Use-Case Intake Process
paras: Every proposed AI system, regardless of tier, follows the same intake gate. The effort at each gate is proportionate to the proposed tier.

sections.heading: 6.1 Stages
paras: Stage 1 — Proposal: submitter completes the Use-Case Intake Form (Appendix A). Triage happens within five working days.
Stage 2 — Tiering: AI & Automation proposes the tier based on data, audience and decision impact. Tier confirmed by Council (Tier 1 and Tier 2) or by Chair delegation (Tier 3).
Stage 3 — Design review: for Tier 1 and Tier 2, architecture, data, model and controls are reviewed. Security, Privacy, Risk and Legal review in parallel.
Stage 4 — Approval: Council vote (Tier 1 unanimous; Tier 2 majority) or Chair approval (Tier 3). Approval captured in the register with scope, limits, monitoring plan and review date.
Stage 5 — Build and validate: proportionate to tier (see §8).
Stage 6 — Deploy: only after the model owner signs the acceptance letter confirming controls are in place.
Stage 7 — Operate: monitor against defined metrics; retrain/retire on defined triggers.
Stage 8 — Decommission: remove access, archive artefacts, update the register.

sections.heading: 7. Model and Tool Approval
paras: Foundation models and AI tools are approved separately from use cases. Once approved for use in the tenant, they can be used by any approved use case consistent with their tier.

sections.heading: 7.2 Adding a new model or tool
paras: Sponsor submits a model/tool onboarding request to AI & Automation including: vendor, contract terms, data flows, residency, training-data posture.
Security, Privacy, Risk, Legal and Procurement review in parallel; AI Council approves or rejects.
Onboarded tools are recorded in the AI tooling register with scope, permitted tiers, and cost controls.
Unapproved generative AI services may not be used with company data or customer data, including free consumer versions.

sections.heading: 8. Model Risk Management
paras: Model risk management (MRM) for AI systems extends the organisation's existing MRM standard (aligned to SR 11-7 and equivalent guidance). The intensity is calibrated to risk tier.

sections.heading: 8.2 Monitoring triggers for re-review
paras: Sustained drift beyond defined thresholds on performance, fairness or drift metrics.
Material model or vendor change (e.g. upgrade to a new foundation model version).
Regulatory change or new guidance.
Incidents attributed to the AI system (see §11).
Scope change (new data, new audience, new decision coverage).

sections.heading: 9. Data Classification for AI
paras: Existing data classification labels (Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted) apply to AI use. The table below maps labels to permitted AI contexts.

Purview sensitivity labels are the enforcement mechanism: M365 Copilot respects labels at retrieval time, and label-based DLP policies block exfiltration of Restricted content into unapproved AI tools.

sections.heading: 10. Acceptable Use Policy (AI)
paras: This policy binds every employee and contractor. M365 Copilot is currently deployed to all users; this policy applies to that rollout in full, as well as to any developer-targeted or custom AI systems.

sections.heading: 10.1 You may
paras: Use M365 Copilot on documents, emails and meetings you already have permission to access, consistent with sensitivity labels.
Use GitHub Copilot Enterprise or Claude Code on Foundry within the scope of the developer Acceptable Use section (see Developer Rollout Plan).
Propose new AI use cases via the intake process — experimentation is encouraged within the framework.

sections.heading: 10.2 You must
paras: Treat AI outputs as drafts; you remain responsible for the work you produce and ship.
Apply sensitivity labels correctly to the documents and records you create.
Disclose to customers when AI has materially shaped a decision that affects them.
Complete required AI literacy training within the timeframe set by People & Culture.

sections.heading: 10.3 You must not
paras: Paste customer PII, payment card data, authentication secrets, or Restricted content into any AI system not specifically approved for that data class.
Use consumer AI services (free ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude consumer apps) with any Internal, Confidential or Restricted company data.
Build or deploy an AI system outside the intake process, including 'shadow' Power Automate flows with AI Builder or unregistered Copilot Studio agents.
Use AI to fabricate records, citations, or evidence, or to impersonate another person without disclosure.

sections.heading: 11. Incident Response for AI
paras: AI incidents use the organisation's existing incident-response runbook with AI-specific extensions. The objective is containment, restoration of trust and learning, not blame.

sections.heading: 11.1 What counts as an AI incident
paras: Any output that causes customer harm, regulatory exposure, or reputational damage.
Data leakage via AI prompts, outputs or indexing.
Material fairness / bias finding in production.
Prompt-injection or model-manipulation event with operational impact.
Failure of a high-risk model (outage, drift beyond thresholds) with downstream impact.

sections.heading: 11.2 Response roles
paras: Incident Commander: Head of AI & Automation or nominated delegate.
Model Owner: accountable for the affected system; leads technical investigation.
Legal, Privacy, Comms, Security: standing responders per runbook.
Regulator contact: General Counsel, with CRO informed.

sections.heading: 11.3 Post-incident
paras: Blameless postmortem within 10 working days.
Corrective actions tracked to closure in the AI register.
AI Council reviews at the next standing meeting; material incidents escalated to ExCo and Board Risk.

sections.heading: 12. Third-Party and Supply Chain
paras: AI introduced through vendors receives the same scrutiny as AI built in-house. Third-party AI is onboarded via the existing vendor-risk process with AI-specific questions.
Vendor AI risk questionnaire (data use, training posture, model provenance, evaluations, incident history).
Contracts include terms on: no training on our data, data residency, breach notification, audit rights, AI-specific warranties and indemnities.
Material changes by the vendor (model upgrade, provider change) trigger re-review.
Approved vendors appear in the AI tooling register alongside in-house systems.

sections.heading: 13. Metrics and Reporting
paras: Reporting runs on three cadences: operational weekly, portfolio monthly, board quarterly.

sections.heading: 14. Review and Change Control
paras: This framework is reviewed annually by the AI Council, or sooner on a material regulatory change (e.g. EU AI Act enforcement phase, updated SARB / CBN guidance).
Proposed changes are submitted as versioned amendments; the framework is re-published with a changelog.
Material deviations from the framework require documented exception approval by the AI Council (Tier 1 / Tier 2) or Chair (Tier 3).

sections.heading: 1. Purpose and Audience
paras: This Playbook is the operational guide for the SOC, the AI & Automation team, and the AI Council Secretary on how AI-related events are detected, triaged, classified, contained and reviewed. It is the third document in the AI control set, sitting alongside the AI Governance Framework v1.0 (policy and accountability) and the AI Control Register v1.0 (controls inventory).
It is not a customer-facing or staff-facing document. The AI Acceptable Use Policy v1.0 §10 is the staff-facing reporting guide; this Playbook is what happens after a report or alert lands.

sections.heading: 3. Monitoring Stack
paras: AI signals from across the estate are funnelled into Microsoft Sentinel, where SOC analysts work them with the same tooling and workflow used for non-AI signals. Specialist consoles (Purview, Defender for Cloud, GitHub) are the source-of-truth for deep investigation.

sections.heading: 4. Alert Catalog and Severities
paras: Each alert in Sentinel has a default severity, the conditions that must be met, and a default response time. SOC may upgrade severity based on context (e.g. customer impact, regulator-relevant content).

sections.heading: 5. Triage Workflow
paras: Every AI alert or report follows the same six steps. SLA clocks start at the moment the alert is created in Sentinel or ServiceNow.

sections.heading: 6. Incident Playbooks
paras: Each playbook follows the same shape: trigger → first 60 minutes → first 24 hours → root-cause → control fix. Playbooks are deliberately short — link to detail in Sentinel runbooks.

sections.heading: PB-1 — Customer or confidential data leakage via M365 Copilot or Foundry
paras: First 60 minutes: confirm the data class involved (PII / financial / credentials). Identify the affected user(s) and the document path. If customer PII is in scope, page the DPO immediately. Disable the offending Copilot session if leakage is in flight; suspend the user account if exfiltration is suspected.

First 24 hours: contain the source — fix the SharePoint oversharing, retract the document, revoke external links, run a Copilot-purge on the affected items, force-recall sent emails. Establish full scope via Purview Audit (who saw what, when, how many).
Root cause: misclassified document, label inheritance failure, oversharing in source SharePoint, prompt designed to extract data, or model behaviour. Identify which class.
Control fix: tune the relevant control (B.01 / B.02 / B.03 / D.01); update the AUP if user behaviour was a contributor; brief the affected business unit.
Notification: DPO assesses POPIA / NDPA / KDPA notification thresholds; GC initiates regulator clock if criteria met (see §8).

sections.heading: PB-2 — Prompt injection / jailbreak / model manipulation
paras: First 60 minutes: confirm the affected endpoint or agent. If a customer-facing system is affected, take it out of service via the kill-switch in the use-case runbook. Capture the offending prompt and response for evidence.
First 24 hours: assess what the injection achieved (data leak? misleading output? action performed?). Re-test with content-safety filters. Patch system prompt / guardrails. Run abuse-test regression.
Root cause: weak system prompt, missing output validation, untrusted retrieval source, model behaviour. Identify class.
Control fix: tighten Foundry content-safety configuration (C.02), re-run prompt-shield checks, add an output validator if appropriate; update detection rule for repeat patterns (D.02).

sections.heading: PB-3 — Unapproved AI tool use
paras: First 60 minutes: identify the user(s) and the tool(s); confirm whether company data was uploaded. Block further connections at the proxy / DfCA. If data was uploaded, escalate to PB-1.
First 24 hours: secure deletion request to the tool provider where applicable; confirm with the user that they understand the AUP §5.3; refer for disciplinary review per AUP §11 if wilful.
Root cause: gap in approved-tool list (user had a real need), gap in egress controls, gap in awareness.
Control fix: tighten egress controls (E.02), update approved-tool list (C.04) if the need is legitimate, send refresher comms; re-attest if a wider gap is found.

sections.heading: PB-4 — Code or secret leakage via developer AI assistant
paras: First 60 minutes: revoke the leaked secret immediately (rotate the key, invalidate the token, change the credential). Identify all systems where the secret was valid. Page the AppSec lead.

First 24 hours: scan for use of the leaked secret; force git-history rewrite if necessary; verify GHAS push-protection should have caught it (and why it didn't); confirm the scope of any code that was sent to a public model.
Root cause: missing pre-commit hook, push-protection bypass, IDE behaviour, or pasted-into-prompt. Identify class.
Control fix: tune GHAS configuration (F.02), tighten pre-commit hooks, refresh developer training.

sections.heading: PB-5 — Spend runaway / consumption anomaly
paras: First 60 minutes: confirm the project, the model and the consumer (workload / pipeline / user). If runaway is active, throttle or stop the workload via Foundry; if a runaway script, kill it.

First 24 hours: identify root cause — bug, prompt loop, malicious workload, mis-sized batch job, model selection error. Quantify financial exposure and confirm whether it is recoverable from Microsoft credits.
Root cause: missing per-model cap, missing budget alert, wrong cost-control configuration, dev environment without auto-stop.
Control fix: confirm H.01–H.03 are operating; introduce a circuit-breaker pattern in the affected pipeline; review architecture if needed.

sections.heading: PB-6 — Prohibited use detected (Tier 4)
paras: First 60 minutes: stop the use case. If it is in production, pull it offline. Brief CISO, GC, DPO and the Head of AI & Automation.

First 24 hours: convene an emergency AI Council (Framework §4.3). Identify: was the use case ever approved? If yes, why was it not flagged as Tier 4? If no, why was it operating? What was the exposure?
Root cause: intake gap, deliberate evasion, ambiguous Tier 4 definition, or change-of-use without re-approval.
Control fix: tighten Framework §6 enforcement; add detection rule (D.02) for the Tier 4 pattern; brief out the lessons.

sections.heading: PB-7 — Model behaviour drift / quality regression
paras: First 60 minutes: confirm the affected use case and the affected metric (accuracy, refusal rate, toxicity, fairness). If it materially affects customers, take the system off-line or revert to the previous version.
First 24 hours: investigate cause — model version change, prompt change, retrieval source change, data drift. Re-run the eval suite on the previous and current configurations.
Root cause: vendor-side model update, change to system prompt, change to retrieval index, real-world drift in inputs.
Control fix: improve evaluation pipeline coverage; introduce a release-gate eval; update monitoring thresholds (D.02 / C.05).

sections.heading: 8. Regulator Notification Thresholds (indicative)
paras: Final assessment is always made by DPO and GC. The clock below is the worst-case external clock; internal escalation begins immediately on P1.

sections.heading: 10. Post-Incident Review (PIR)
paras: Every P1 / P2 incident is reviewed in writing within 5 business days. P3 incidents within 10. P4 events are aggregated monthly. Reviews are blameless — the goal is to fix the system.
Timeline — what happened, in clock time, with the data sources used to reconstruct it.
Impact — customers, employees, financials, regulator exposure.
Root cause — technical, process, control or human; the 5-whys are applied.
What worked — controls that fired, decisions that were quick and right.
What didn't — gaps in detection, response, communication.
Actions — owner, due date, target control to update; tracked through to closure in ServiceNow.
Lessons — short briefing for staff; updates to AUP / Control Register / this Playbook as needed.

sections.heading: How to Use This Document
paras: This document does two things: it captures the information needed to bring an AI use case to the AI Council, and it scores the use case against six risk dimensions to propose a Tier.
Submitters complete Part A (intake) and Part B (self-assessed scoring), then send to the AI & Automation intake inbox.
AI & Automation triages within five working days and confirms or adjusts the Tier.
Council approves Tier 1 / 2; Chair confirms Tier 3; Tier 4 is escalated to ExCo.
The completed form is filed in the use-case register and becomes part of the audit trail.

Triggers for raising an intake: any new AI capability touching company data; a material change to an existing AI system; a new vendor product where AI is a material feature; a citizen-built agent intended to be published beyond the builder.

sections.heading: 10. Sign-offs and Dependencies
paras: PART B — TIER SCORING RUBRIC

sections.heading: B.1 Purpose and Method
paras: The rubric scores a use case across six dimensions. Each dimension is scored 0 / 1 / 3 / 5. The total score determines the proposed Tier per the mapping in §B.3. The rubric is a guide, not a guarantee — Council may override with documented rationale.
Six dimensions: customer impact, regulatory exposure, data sensitivity, decision autonomy, reversibility, scale.
Score per dimension: 0 = none / negligible; 1 = low; 3 = moderate; 5 = high.
Total score range: 0–30. Tier mapping in §B.3.
Some triggers force Tier 1 regardless of total (e.g. credit decision, AML decision, customer-facing autonomous action) — see §B.4.
Some patterns force Tier 4 (prohibited) — see §B.5.

sections.heading: Dimension 1 — Customer Impact
paras: How directly does the AI affect customers?

sections.heading: Dimension 2 — Regulatory Exposure
paras: What regulatory regime does the use case touch, and how prescriptively?

sections.heading: Dimension 3 — Data Sensitivity
paras: Highest data classification reaching the AI system, including via retrieval.

sections.heading: Dimension 4 — Decision Autonomy
paras: How much does the AI act on its own, vs. recommend to a human?

sections.heading: Dimension 5 — Reversibility
paras: How quickly and cheaply can a wrong AI action be undone?

sections.heading: Dimension 6 — Scale
paras: How many users / customers / events are affected?

sections.heading: B.3 Total Score → Tier
paras: If the total falls in T2 but a forcing trigger applies (§B.4), the case is uplifted to T1. If a Tier 4 pattern applies (§B.5), the case is rejected at intake.

sections.heading: B.4 Forcing Triggers — Auto-Uplift to T1
paras: Regardless of total score, the following force a Tier 1 classification:
Use case adjudicates a credit decision.
Use case adjudicates a fraud or AML alert.
Use case prices a customer product, including discount or fee waiver.
Use case takes autonomous customer-facing action (sends a binding communication, executes a transaction, files a regulatory return).
Use case adjudicates an HR decision (hiring, promotion, dismissal, grievance outcome).
Use case affects market activity (trading, hedging, pricing of securities).
Use case acts on special-category personal data.
Independent validator or DPO has flagged a heightened concern.

sections.heading: B.5 Tier 4 Patterns — Prohibited at Intake
paras: The following are not approved at Council level. Any exception requires ExCo approval with documented mitigations.
Fully autonomous credit decisions without human review.
Behavioural scoring of employees or surveillance of communications without explicit lawful basis and consultation.
Emotion or affect recognition in hiring, lending, or customer-service triage.
Covert AI — undisclosed AI in communications where the recipient would reasonably assume a human.
Social-scoring of customers (general behavioural scoring not tied to a regulated, justified outcome).
Use of customer data to train external foundation models.

paras: Three illustrative cases. The aim is to show the rubric in use, not to predict the outcome of any real case.

sections.heading: 0. Purpose and How to Use This DDQ
paras: This Questionnaire is used to assess any third-party product, service or component that uses artificial intelligence and that will touch the organisation's data, customers, systems or staff. It is required:
Before contracting with any new AI vendor.
At renewal of any existing AI vendor contract.
When an existing approved vendor introduces a new AI feature that materially affects how our data is processed.
When a non-AI vendor enables an AI feature in a product we already use (very common).

It is co-owned by the AI & Automation function, the CISO and the DPO. It feeds into the AI Use-Case Intake (where the vendor is part of a use case) and into the standard third-party risk-management process. Findings are summarised on the front page (§A) for sign-off; detail follows in §1–§10.

sections.heading: 0.2 Instructions for vendor
paras: Provide written answers to every question; mark N/A only where a question genuinely does not apply (e.g. a question about model fine-tuning if the product does not allow it).
Attach evidence (certifications, policies, audit reports, architecture diagrams, white papers) and reference each by short ID in the Evidence column.
Where the AI feature is provided by a sub-processor (Azure OpenAI, Anthropic via API, OpenAI direct, Google Vertex, AWS Bedrock, etc.), answer for the sub-processor where indicated; do not assume.
Be explicit about regional differences. Where a control or commitment differs by deployment region, name the regions and explain.
Sign and date the cover-letter attestation that the responses are true and complete to the best of the vendor's knowledge.

Where the vendor underpins a Tier 1 use case: ExCo notification regardless of RAG.

paras: GitHub Copilot Rollout Plan
Pilot, Evaluate, Scale
Fintech deployment • Under 200 developers • Microsoft & AI Foundry stack
Version 1.1 • Head of AI & Automation • Classification: Internal

sections.heading: 1. Executive Summary
paras: This plan sets out how we will roll out GitHub Copilot to our engineering organisation in a way that is safe, measurable, and defensible to the board, our regulators, and our customers. The intent is to unlock material developer-productivity gains while meeting the controls expected of a regulated fintech.

We will adopt GitHub Copilot Enterprise as the standard developer-assistance tool. We will run an 8 to 12 week pilot with a single cohort of 40 to 60 engineers across one or two teams, measure outcomes against a defined baseline, and scale to the full engineering population (under 200 developers) over the following quarter.

In parallel, we will run a second, smaller pilot of Claude Code on Microsoft Foundry against the same cohort and the same metrics, so that our choice of agentic coding tool is data-led rather than vendor-led. Claude models are now available through Microsoft Foundry under our existing Azure agreement (see Appendix C).

The programme is sized for our footprint: one wave after the pilot is realistic, governance overhead is kept light, and the pilot doubles as our evidence base for the AI Council, risk function and external auditors.

sections.heading: 1.1 Expected Outcomes
paras: 15 to 30 percent increase in developer throughput, measured through PR velocity and cycle time, comparable with published industry results.
Measurable reduction in time spent on boilerplate, repetitive tests, documentation and refactoring tasks.
Improved onboarding: new-joiner time-to-first-PR reduced.
Higher code-quality signal through integrated Copilot Code Review and Autofix on security findings.
A documented head-to-head evaluation of GitHub Copilot Enterprise versus Claude Code on Foundry, so tool choice is evidence-based.
Zero tolerance outcomes preserved: no incidents involving source-code exfiltration, no IP infringement events, no production incidents caused by AI-generated code reaching customers unreviewed.

sections.heading: 2. Licensing Decision
paras: GitHub Copilot is offered at several tiers. For a regulated fintech, Copilot Enterprise is the appropriate choice. The recommendation below explains why.

sections.heading: 2.1 Recommendation
paras: Procure Copilot Enterprise for the pilot cohort (40 to 60 seats) and scale to the full engineering population in the second wave. The delta versus Business is material: private-repo grounding, knowledge bases, custom instructions, granular content exclusion and richer analytics are the capabilities a regulated fintech needs to deploy AI responsibly and to evidence its value.
GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS) should be procured in parallel to activate Copilot Autofix and to provide the secret-scanning and CodeQL controls that the AI Council will depend on.

In parallel, run a smaller Claude Code on Microsoft Foundry pilot (10 to 15 seats) inside the same cohort. Claude is now available as a Foundry model under MACC, which removes the separate vendor onboarding burden. Appendix C sets out the structure, controls and decision criteria for that parallel track.

sections.heading: 3. Data, IP and Regulatory Configuration
paras: Before any seat is assigned, the following configuration and sign-offs must be in place. This is the non-negotiable baseline.

sections.heading: 3.1 Tenant and Data Handling
paras: Enterprise-level policy: prompts, suggestions and usage data are not used to train foundation models. Documented in contract addendum.
Residency: use a region that satisfies data-residency obligations in our markets. Where EU-hosted processing is required, enable the EU data residency option for GitHub Enterprise Cloud.
Retention of prompt telemetry set to the minimum required to operate the service; audit-relevant events exported to our own log estate.
Public-code matching filter ON at the organisation level. Enables IP indemnification.

sections.heading: 3.2 Content Exclusions
paras: Copilot content exclusions are applied at repository level to prevent the extension from reading highly sensitive code paths:
Repositories holding cryptographic keys, payment processing, fraud rules engines.
Repositories holding model training scripts that reference customer data.
Any repository labelled Restricted under the data-classification policy.

sections.heading: 3.3 Identity and Access
paras: Copilot seats assigned via Entra ID groups, not individuals. One group per engineering domain.
Conditional access on GitHub Enterprise Cloud login: compliant device, MFA, trusted location.
Quarterly access review to reclaim unused seats.

sections.heading: 3.4 Legal and Compliance Sign-off Checklist
paras: Data-Protection Impact Assessment completed under POPIA / NDPA / KDPA as applicable, signed by DPO.
Vendor due-diligence renewed and GitHub onboarded through the third-party risk process.
Acceptable-use policy for Copilot reviewed by Legal and acknowledged by each user.
Model-risk owner appointed (Head of AI & Automation) and Copilot entered in the AI use-case register.
Works-council or employee-representation consultation completed where required.

sections.heading: 4.1 Cohort Selection
paras: Pick a cohort that is big enough to produce a defensible signal but small enough to support hands-on. For an organisation under 200 engineers, 40 to 60 seats across one or two teams is the right size.
One product team writing a mainstream language we support (for example Python or TypeScript backend).
One platform or DevOps team whose work is a mix of IaC, pipelines and tooling.
Representation across seniority: seniors stress-test limits, juniors reveal onboarding value, tech leads set norms.
Exclude teams under active regulator remediation from the pilot; include them in wave 2.

sections.heading: 4.2 Duration
paras: Eight weeks for measurement, plus a two-week warm-up and a two-week read-out. Twelve calendar weeks end to end.

sections.heading: 4.3 Baseline Metrics
paras: Metrics are captured for four weeks before Copilot is switched on, from the same cohort, so that we are comparing like with like.
Avoid lines-of-code as a metric. It rewards the wrong behaviour and is uncorrelated with value.

sections.heading: 4.4 Pilot Governance
paras: Weekly pilot stand-up with engineering leads, AI & Automation and Security.
Bi-weekly AI Council update.
Issue log covering quality concerns, IP concerns, and adoption friction.
At week 8, formal read-out with recommendation: expand, continue pilot, or stop.

sections.heading: 5. Training and Enablement
paras: Training is tiered so that each audience gets what they actually need, and no one is forced to sit through material that is not relevant to their role.

sections.heading: 5.1 Champion Network
paras: Three to five Copilot champions embedded in the pilot teams.
They run weekly clinics, curate prompt patterns, and surface issues to the AI & Automation function.
Champions expand to one per team in wave 2.

sections.heading: 6. Acceptable Use Policy
paras: The acceptable-use policy is short and practical. Every Copilot user acknowledges it before seat assignment.

sections.heading: 6.1 You may
paras: Use Copilot to write, refactor, test, document and review code inside approved repositories.
Use Copilot Chat to explain code, generate tests, propose migrations and help with debugging.
Use Copilot Code Review as an additional reviewer on pull requests.
Use Claude Code on Microsoft Foundry for the same purposes if you are a member of the Claude Code pilot cohort (see Appendix C).

sections.heading: 6.2 You must
paras: Treat every AI-generated suggestion as a draft. You are responsible for the code you merge.
Run tests, linters and security scanners before merging.
Apply the same review bar you would apply to a human colleague's code, or higher.
Cite externally-sourced patterns appropriately and comply with licence obligations.

sections.heading: 6.3 You must not
paras: Paste production customer data, secrets, or Restricted-classified content into Copilot Chat or Claude Code.
Use Copilot or Claude Code to generate code that implements controls you are not authorised to change (for example fraud rules, AML logic).
Bypass security scanners, code-review, or deployment controls because 'the AI said it was fine'.

Use consumer AI services (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude consumer apps) with company code. Use our sanctioned Copilot and Foundry paths instead — GitHub Copilot Enterprise or Claude on Microsoft Foundry are the only approved channels.

sections.heading: 9. Scale-out Decision Criteria
paras: At the week-13 read-out, the decision to scale, continue or stop is made against explicit thresholds. This prevents the pilot from becoming open-ended and gives the board a clean yes or no.

sections.heading: 9.1 Scale
paras: Copilot acceptance rate greater than 25% sustained across the final four weeks.
Weekly active use greater than 70% of cohort.
PR review time or lead time reduced vs. baseline (directional).
No material security or IP incident attributable to Copilot.
Developer experience score improved or stable, positive qualitative feedback majority.

sections.heading: 9.2 Continue pilot
paras: Signals are ambiguous: use a further four weeks to sharpen enablement, content exclusions or cohort composition.

sections.heading: 9.3 Stop
paras: Material incident: code leakage, IP exposure, regulator intervention.
Sustained negative developer experience.
Adoption stuck below 30% despite enablement effort.

sections.heading: 10. Governance Integration
paras: Copilot and Claude Code on Foundry are registered as AI use cases in the AI register: use-case owner, risk tier, data classes, approved model providers, evaluation notes.
AI Council reviews Copilot and Claude Code posture quarterly once scaled.
Incidents involving AI-assisted code follow the standard incident-response runbook with an AI addendum describing any retraining or configuration changes made.
Board reporting: included in the AI scorecard alongside adoption and value metrics.
