sections.heading: 1. Executive Summary
paras: This document defines the reference architecture for the sandbox and non-production environments that will host AI-assisted software development across the organisation. It is designed to let development teams experiment with AI tooling, generative-AI applications, and bespoke agents at the speed the business expects, while preserving the data-protection, model-risk, and operational-resilience controls that a regulated fintech is held to.

The architecture is built on our approved Microsoft stack. Developer environments are delivered through GitHub Codespaces, Microsoft Dev Box and Azure Deployment Environments. AI experimentation and model deployment run inside Azure AI Foundry hubs and projects. All of this sits within an Azure landing zone whose controls are enforced automatically via Azure Policy, Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft Purview and Microsoft Defender for Cloud.

The design intent is opinionated: the paved road should be the fastest and easiest path for engineers, so that shadow IT and shadow AI have no reason to exist. Every sandbox is time-bound, cost-capped, identity-gated, network-segmented, and isolated from production customer data. No production data ever enters a sandbox; synthetic or masked datasets are provided through a governed pipeline.

sections.heading: 2.1 Objectives
paras: Enable self-service provisioning of development and AI experimentation environments in under 10 minutes.
Eliminate shadow AI by providing a sanctioned path that is faster than unsanctioned alternatives.
Contain blast radius - sandboxes cannot reach production data, production networks, or unapproved model providers.
Satisfy model-risk, data-protection and third-party controls expected by financial regulators across our operating markets.
Provide a clean evidence trail for auditors: who provisioned what, what data was used, what models were evaluated, who approved deployment.

sections.heading: 2.2 Design Principles
paras: Secure by default. Guardrails are enforced at the platform layer, not left to the developer. Policy violations fail at deployment time, not in production.
Ephemeral by default. Every sandbox has an expiry date. Long-lived environments require explicit justification and approval.
Least privilege and just-in-time. Elevated access is granted through Entra PIM for a bounded window and recorded.
Data stays where it belongs. Sandboxes consume synthetic or masked data only; egress to external model providers is allow-listed.
Observable. Every environment emits telemetry to a central log estate so that drift, cost and misuse are visible.
Paved road over picket fences. The sanctioned path is the fastest path; controls succeed because they are easier to follow than to work around.

sections.heading: 3. Reference Architecture Overview
paras: The sandbox estate is organised as four complementary environment types, each solving a different problem. All four are governed by the same identity, data, and policy planes.

sections.heading: 3.2 Layered View
paras: The architecture is organised as seven layers, each with clear ownership:
Platform layer: Azure landing zone, management groups, subscription vending, networking, key management, logging.
Identity and access layer: Microsoft Entra ID, conditional access, PIM, workload identities.
Data and governance layer: Microsoft Purview catalogue, sensitivity labels, DLP, synthetic data service.
Compute layer: AKS, App Service, Container Apps, Azure Functions, Foundry compute.
AI platform layer: Azure AI Foundry hub, project, model catalogue, evaluations, content safety.
Developer experience layer: Codespaces, Dev Box, ADE catalogue, GitHub Copilot, Visual Studio, VS Code.
Observability layer: Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, Microsoft Sentinel, Defender for Cloud, Cost Management.

sections.heading: 4. Azure Tenant and Subscription Topology
paras: All non-production AI and developer activity lives under a dedicated management group hierarchy that is isolated from production. This separation is the single most important control in the architecture: it makes it structurally impossible for a sandbox mistake to impact a customer.

sections.heading: 4.1 Management Group Hierarchy
paras: Tenant Root
Platform - shared services, connectivity, identity, management
Landing Zones - production workloads
Corp (connected)
Online (internet-facing)
Sandboxes - non-production, time-bound
Dev - team development subscriptions
AI-Experiments - Foundry hubs and project subscriptions
Individual - per-engineer playground (low spend cap)
Decommissioned - retired subscriptions held for audit

sections.heading: 4.2 Subscription Vending
paras: Subscriptions are never requested by ticket. They are vended by an automated pipeline triggered from a self-service portal. The vending pipeline attaches the subscription to the correct management group, applies the baseline policy initiative, tags the subscription with owner, cost-centre and expiry date, and registers it in the central subscription inventory.

sections.heading: 4.3 Isolation Rules
paras: Sandbox subscriptions cannot peer with production virtual networks.
Outbound egress is routed through the central firewall with an allow-list of approved destinations.
No production data stores are reachable from sandbox private endpoints.
Cross-subscription role assignments into production are explicitly denied.

sections.heading: 5. Governance and Policy Guardrails
paras: Controls are enforced through an Azure Policy initiative assigned at the Sandboxes management group. Developers see policy failures as clear deployment errors, not as a security team interrupting their work.

sections.heading: 5.2 Tagging Schema
paras: Every sandbox resource is tagged at creation. Missing tags cause deployment to fail. Expiry drives the clean-up runbook.
Owner - Entra UPN of the responsible engineer.
CostCentre - finance code used for show-back.
Project - business project identifier.
Expiry - ISO date after which automated tear-down runs.
DataClass - Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted (sandbox ceiling is Internal).
AIUseCase - registered use-case ID (required for any Foundry project).

sections.heading: 5.3 Cost Guardrails
paras: Subscription budget with alerts at 50%, 80%, 100%.
At 100%, Azure Policy disables further resource creation and non-critical compute is suspended.
Individual playgrounds carry a hard monthly cap set by the AI Council.
GPU quota requires a named justification and is time-bound.

sections.heading: 6.1 Identity
paras: All human access via Microsoft Entra ID with phishing-resistant MFA.
Privileged roles (Contributor and above on sandbox subscriptions) granted through PIM with a maximum 8-hour window.
Workload identities (managed identities and workload federated credentials) are always preferred over secrets.
Copilot, Foundry and ADE access gated by conditional access policies: compliant device, trusted location, MFA.

sections.heading: 6.2 Access Patterns
paras: Engineers: Reader at subscription, Contributor at resource-group level of their own sandbox.
Tech leads: Contributor at team subscription for the active sprint, via PIM.
Platform engineers: Owner at the Sandboxes management group, via PIM, with break-glass logged.
No standing Owner roles on sandbox subscriptions.

sections.heading: 6.3 Network
paras: All sandbox virtual networks are spoked off a non-production hub. The hub hosts a central Azure Firewall, DNS, and egress points. There is no peering to production hubs.
Private endpoints for PaaS data services.
Service endpoints blocked in favour of private endpoints.
Egress allow-list includes: GitHub, Azure public services, approved model providers, approved package registries.
Web traffic logged and retained for 90 days; DNS queries logged to Sentinel.

sections.heading: 7. Data Handling and Privacy
paras: Data protection is the single control that most commonly fails in AI sandboxes. The principle is simple: production customer data never enters a sandbox. Engineers who need realistic data use synthetic or masked substitutes provisioned through a governed pipeline.

sections.heading: 7.1 Data Classification in Sandboxes
paras: Public - permitted without restriction.
Internal - permitted (ceiling for standard sandboxes).
Confidential - only with an approved exception and additional controls.
Restricted / PII / PCI - not permitted. No exceptions.

sections.heading: 7.2 Synthetic and Masked Data
paras: Synthetic datasets generated from production schemas using an approved tool (e.g. SDV, Tonic, or an internal generator) and validated for absence of re-identification risk.
Masked datasets produced by a pipeline that applies deterministic pseudonymisation of direct identifiers, generalisation of quasi-identifiers, and removal of free-text PII.
Both are published to sandbox storage accounts that are allow-listed in the egress policy and labelled via Purview.

sections.heading: 7.3 Regulatory Alignment
paras: The architecture is designed to satisfy the data-protection obligations we are subject to across our operating markets. Key instruments include:
South Africa - POPIA (Protection of Personal Information Act). Regulator: Information Regulator.
Nigeria - Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and NDP Regulation. Regulator: NDPC.
Kenya - Data Protection Act 2019. Regulator: ODPC.
Ghana - Data Protection Act 2012. Regulator: DPC.
Egypt - Personal Data Protection Law. Regulator: PDPC.
Cross-border - AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention).

Where a use case processes personal data, the AI Council will map it against the lawful basis, cross-border transfer, and breach-notification obligations in the relevant jurisdiction prior to deployment.

sections.heading: 7.4 Data Loss Prevention
paras: Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels applied to Foundry project artefacts, datasets and outputs.
Endpoint DLP on Dev Boxes and corporate endpoints blocks upload of labelled content to unsanctioned destinations.
Defender for Cloud Apps flags anomalous AI-tool use and blocks unsanctioned generative-AI endpoints.

sections.heading: 8. AI-Specific Controls (Azure AI Foundry)
paras: Azure AI Foundry is the sanctioned environment for all generative-AI development. The hub-and-project pattern maps naturally onto a fintech governance model: the hub holds shared infrastructure, security and connectivity; each project is a workspace scoped to a business use case and approved by the AI Council.

sections.heading: 8.1 Hub Design
paras: One production hub per business domain (for example Customer, Risk, Operations).
Shared connections to approved model providers configured at hub level.
Centrally managed content safety, customer-managed keys, private networking.
Foundry audit logs streamed to the central Log Analytics workspace and Sentinel.

sections.heading: 8.2 Project Controls
paras: Each project requires a registered use case ID and an approved data classification.
Model catalogue restricted to approved models; new entries require an AI Council decision.
Prompt flow evaluations mandatory before any deployment beyond the sandbox stage.
Content safety filters enabled by default on all deployed endpoints.
Responsible AI dashboard evidence (fairness, explainability, error analysis) stored as part of the model card.

sections.heading: 8.3 Approved Model Providers
paras: Sandbox Foundry projects may consume models from the following approved providers, subject to data classification limits set by the AI Council:
Azure OpenAI Service (primary).
Foundry-hosted open-weight models (Llama, Phi, Mistral) deployed into our tenant.
Foundry-partner models with contractual commitments that prompts and completions are not used for training.
No direct calls to consumer endpoints (for example chat.openai.com, gemini.google.com) from sandbox networks.

sections.heading: 8.4 Evaluation Requirements
paras: Groundedness and relevance scored on a curated evaluation set for any RAG application.
Safety evaluation (harmful content, PII leakage, jailbreak resistance) mandatory for customer-facing or decisioning use cases.
Red-team assessment required for any use case classified High-risk by the AI Council.
Evaluation artefacts retained for the regulatory retention window.

sections.heading: 9.1 Provisioning
paras: Engineer opens an intake form in the self-service portal (backed by the AI use-case register).
Automated checks: Entra group membership, training completion, data-classification declaration.
Subscription vended, catalogue template deployed, tags applied, expiry set.
Engineer receives environment details, a scoped RBAC role and a link to the deprovisioning runbook.

sections.heading: 9.2 Usage
paras: Environment is monitored for idle time, cost drift and policy compliance.
Weekly cost digest emailed to owner and cost-centre manager.
Expiry extension requires justification and is capped at two extensions of 30 days each.

sections.heading: 9.3 Deprovisioning
paras: Seven days before expiry, owner receives the first reminder.
On expiry, automated tear-down runs: compute destroyed, data archived or deleted per retention policy, tags retained.
Subscription moved to the Decommissioned management group for an audit hold period.
Final clean-up after the hold period releases the subscription.

sections.heading: 10. Monitoring, Observability and Audit
paras: All sandbox subscriptions send platform logs, activity logs and diagnostic logs to a central Log Analytics workspace.
Microsoft Sentinel analytic rules detect: unsanctioned model endpoint egress, data exfiltration patterns, anomalous Copilot use, privilege escalation.
Defender for Cloud secure-score baseline target: 85%+ across sandbox subscriptions.
Foundry audit trail (prompts, completions metadata, evaluations) retained for the regulatory retention period.
Quarterly access review via Entra Access Reviews for all sandbox-adjacent roles.

sections.heading: 11. Cost Management
paras: Daily cost ingestion to a Power BI cost dashboard with per-project, per-owner and per-use-case views.
Show-back model: cost-centre attribution is enforced via tagging and visible to engineering leadership.
GPU, Foundry deployments, and LLM token spend broken out as separate cost pillars.
Automated anomaly alerts on 25%+ week-over-week cost movement.

sections.heading: 12. Fintech-Specific Considerations
paras: Regulatory expectations on financial institutions using AI converge on a small number of themes. The following map those themes to specific controls in this architecture.

sections.heading: 13. Roles and Responsibilities
paras: R = Responsible, A = Accountable, C = Consulted, I = Informed.

sections.heading: 14. Success Metrics
paras: Time to first running sandbox: target under 10 minutes, measured monthly.
Share of developers using sanctioned sandbox path: target above 95%.
Policy compliance: target 100% of sandbox subscriptions on the baseline initiative, zero non-compliant resources aged more than 24 hours.
Cost efficiency: sandbox spend as percentage of total non-production Azure spend, monitored, with a defined upper threshold.
Shadow-AI detections trending toward zero quarter on quarter.
Security events from sandboxes reaching production: target zero.

sections.heading: Executive Summary
paras: This Playbook sets out how vendor development teams operating under staff-augmentation arrangements use AI coding tools — primarily GitHub Copilot Enterprise and Claude Code on Azure AI Foundry — to accelerate the delivery of code and features for the organisation.

The premise is simple: under staff augmentation, vendor developers work as part of our teams, on our tickets, in our repositories. The same productivity uplift we want for internal engineers is available to them, and at lower marginal cost. But the trust boundary is different. Vendor personnel are not employees. The contracts that govern them, the controls applied to them, and the way we measure their output need to reflect that — not by treating them as suspects, but by being explicit about what is shared, what is permitted and what is not.
Three commitments frame the approach.

Commitment 1 — Vendor developers operating on our codebase use the AI tools we provide, signed in with identities we issue, on environments we control, and to the same Acceptable Use Policy our employees follow.

Commitment 2 — Productivity gains from AI accrue to the organisation, not to vendor margin. Hourly-rate engagements are managed down. Fixed-scope engagements are rebased. The mechanism is in the SOW Addendum.

Commitment 3 — Quality, security and IP standards are not relaxed because AI wrote the code. Vendor developers are accountable for what they commit; vendors are contractually accountable for what their developers ship.

sections.heading: 1.1 Purpose
paras: To enable vendor development teams to use AI coding assistants productively and safely, with controls that match the staff-augmentation engagement model and contracts that capture the value of the productivity uplift.

sections.heading: 1.2 Scope
paras: All vendor personnel placed with the organisation under staff-augmentation arrangements who write or review code on our codebase.
All AI coding tools and AI-enabled development workflows used in the course of that work.
Both off-shore and on-site delivery; both individual contractors via vendor and full vendor squads.

sections.heading: 1.3 Out of scope (covered separately)
paras: Fixed-price SOW deliverables where a vendor delivers a feature for an agreed price — different commercial logic; addressed in a separate forthcoming guidance.
Managed-service squads with vendor-owned tech leads — addressed separately.
Internal-employee use of AI coding tools — covered in the GitHub Copilot Rollout Plan and the AI Acceptable Use Policy.

sections.heading: 2. The Opportunity and the Constraint
paras: Vendor staff augmentation is, by headcount, a significant share of our delivery capacity. A 10–20% productivity uplift across that population is one of the highest-leverage moves available — directly comparable to the case made for internal engineers in the GitHub Copilot Rollout Plan.

The constraint is that vendor personnel are not employees. We do not control hiring, exit, equipment or training. We do contractually control how they work on our systems. AI tooling sits squarely on that line: we provision the tool, we enforce the policy, the vendor accepts the contractual terms, and the individual attests to the policy before access is granted.

sections.heading: 3. Operating Model — Staff Augmentation Specifics
paras: Under staff augmentation, the vendor developer is integrated into our team. They use our tickets, our repositories, our pipelines, our review process. The AI tooling fits the same pattern: ours.

sections.heading: 3.1 Principles
paras: Single source of tooling. Vendor developers use the AI tools we provide. They do not use personal Copilot accounts, personal Claude / ChatGPT, or any vendor-provided AI tool on our codebase.
Single identity. Vendor developers sign in with Entra ID identities issued by us, scoped to the engagement. No shared accounts, no service accounts.
Single policy. The AI Acceptable Use Policy v1.0 binds vendor developers in the same way it binds employees, via attestation.
Single environment. Vendor developers work on Microsoft Dev Box / Azure Deployment Environments where applicable; their personal laptops do not host our code.
Single review process. AI-assisted code from a vendor developer goes through the same human review and pre-merge checks as any other code.
Outcome-based commercial. We expect productivity uplift; we measure it; we rebase the engagement to capture the value (see §11).

sections.heading: 3.2 What changes vs. internal engineers, and what doesn't
4. Tooling
paras: Tooling for vendor developers mirrors the internal stack, with two notable differences: identity provisioning and Dev Box-first device strategy.

sections.heading: 4.1 Approved AI tools for vendor developers
4.2 Prohibited
paras: Personal Copilot, personal Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini / any consumer AI account on our code, in our IDE, or on our managed device.
Vendor-provided AI tools (Copilot alternatives, code-review bots, AI-enabled IDEs) on our code without explicit approval via the Vendor DDQ + Council intake.
Pasting our code into any AI surface other than the approved tools, including for the purpose of asking the model a question.
Using AI tools through a browser plugin, browser extension, IDE extension or terminal wrapper that is not part of the approved-tool stack.

sections.heading: 4.3 Devices
paras: Default: Microsoft Dev Box, with Visual Studio / IntelliJ / VS Code pre-configured, GitHub Copilot Enterprise enabled, no local code persistence, auto-stop in off-hours.
Where Dev Box is not viable (specific tooling, performance): vendor-managed laptop enrolled in our Intune; full disk encryption; only approved IDE extensions.
Personal devices: never. No exceptions for staff-aug arrangements.

sections.heading: 5. Vendor Developer Onboarding Flow
paras: A new vendor developer reaches a productive AI-enabled state inside 5 working days from contract signature. The process is standardised so any new vendor squad can be stood up against the same runbook.

sections.heading: 6. Governance — How the Existing Controls Apply to Vendor Developers
paras: The existing AI Governance Framework, AUP, Control Register and Monitoring Playbook all extend to vendor developers. This section is not a new control set; it is a map showing how the existing controls land on the vendor population.

sections.heading: 7. Quality and Code Review — The Bar Doesn't Drop
paras: AI-assisted code is faster to write. It is not faster to review unless reviewers are equally tooled. Quality and security expectations are unchanged.
Branch protection enforces a human reviewer on every PR. Branch protection rules are tenant-managed and cannot be bypassed by repository owners.

GHAS pre-merge checks (CodeQL, secret scanning, push protection, dependency review) must pass before merge. High-severity Copilot Autofix recommendations must be resolved or explicitly waived with senior approval.
Copilot Code Review is enabled on PRs, providing an automated first-pass review that complements the human reviewer.
Security-critical paths (authn, authz, crypto, payment routing) require two senior reviewers, one of whom is internal, irrespective of who wrote the code.
Vendor developer commit volume is monitored. Sudden volume increases trigger a quality spot-check rather than a celebration.
Test coverage and mutation-testing thresholds are unchanged. AI does not earn an exemption from tests.

sections.heading: 8.1 Code ownership
paras: All work product produced under the engagement — including AI-assisted code, prompts and any artefacts — vests in the customer (us) per the master agreement. The SOW Addendum re-states this with specific reference to AI-assisted output to remove ambiguity.

Vendor warrants that AI-assisted output does not knowingly introduce third-party IP or copyleft-licensed content; copyright filter / public-code matching must be enabled in GitHub Copilot Enterprise (Control F.04).
Vendor and individual developer indemnities cover IP claims arising from AI-assisted output to the extent the vendor controls or accepts the tooling configuration.

sections.heading: 8.2 Sensitive data
paras: No customer PII, no production secrets, no production data of any kind enters AI prompts — same rule as for internal engineers (AUP §8.3). Test data must be synthetic or pseudonymised.
Vendor developers cannot move code outside our environment to use a different AI tool. The Dev Box / managed device pattern enforces this technically; the SOW Addendum enforces it contractually.
Vendor own-AI-tooling proposals follow the AI Vendor & Third-Party DDQ. Default approved-tool list does not include vendor-provided AI.

sections.heading: 8.3 Identity and offboarding
paras: Vendor must provide a Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) feed: starts and exits within 24 hours; role changes within 5 working days. Manual notification by email is not acceptable for ongoing engagements.
Identity expiry on engagement end-date is automatic; renewal requires positive confirmation from the vendor account manager and the squad lead.
Quarterly access reviews on guest accounts; dormant identities (no sign-in for 30 days) are auto-disabled and reclaimed.

sections.heading: 9. Productivity Measurement
paras: Productivity is measured at squad level, not individual level. The point is to show whether the AI investment is paying for itself in vendor cost; it is not to performance-rank individual contractors.

sections.heading: 9.2 Baseline
paras: Two sprints of pre-AI baseline data captured for every squad before AI tooling is enabled. No exceptions.
Baselines are signed off by the squad lead and the vendor account manager; once signed, they are the reference point for the engagement.
Squad-level data is the unit of measurement. Individual-level data is collected for hygiene but not used for performance ranking of vendor staff.

sections.heading: 9.3 Reporting
paras: Weekly squad metrics dashboard reviewed by squad lead and vendor account manager.
Monthly vendor scorecard reviewed at Vendor Service Review (VSR) — productivity uplift, quality, AI tooling adoption, incident count.
Quarterly vendor review at the AI Council with the Head of Software Engineering and Procurement — strategic view, commercial implications.

sections.heading: 10. Change Management with Vendors
paras: Vendors will not always be enthusiastic — productivity gains that flow to the customer reduce billed hours. Treat the conversation as a partnership reset, not a takeaway.
Lead with the customer's strategic intent: faster delivery, better quality, longer-term relationship for vendors who help us win.

Acknowledge the commercial reality: hourly-rate engagements that become more efficient mean fewer billed hours; the vendor's value-share comes through scope expansion, longer engagements, and reputation, not through inflated hours.
Co-design the squad-level metrics with the vendor account manager. They have to defend the targets internally; getting buy-in is faster than imposing.
Be explicit about red lines: no AI tools we don't approve, no code outside our environment, no shortcuts on review. Vendors who push back on these are signalling a problem.
Recognise progress publicly. A vendor squad that hits the productivity targets gets named in the quarterly Council review and is first in line for new work.

sections.heading: 11. Commercial Implications and Value Capture
paras: This is the part that vendor account managers will read first. Be explicit about how value is shared.

These mechanics are templated in the Vendor SOW Addendum that accompanies this Playbook. Procurement runs the addendum into existing master agreements; new agreements include the addendum from the start.

sections.heading: 15. Success Criteria
paras: Pilot exit (Day 90): two vendor squads delivering against the productivity uplift targets in §9.1, with no quality regression and no material incidents.
Year-1 (month 12): all in-scope vendor staff-aug squads using the approved AI tooling, attested AUP at 100%, monthly vendor scorecard standing, productivity uplift of 10–15% measured at squad level.
Commercial: at least 50% of in-scope engagements rebased or rate-reviewed to capture productivity gains; documented value-capture by squad.
Risk: zero P1 vendor-AI incidents; less than 3 P3 vendor-AI incidents per quarter; vendor audit rights exercised at least once per Year-1.

sections.heading: 'Can our developers use their own GitHub Copilot subscription if it's faster?'
paras: No. Personal Copilot accounts are blocked at the IDE / repository level. Use the Customer-provisioned Copilot Enterprise seat assigned through the engagement.

sections.heading: 'Can we use ChatGPT to debug a tricky issue if we don't paste any of your code?'
paras: No. The risk of incidental code or context leakage is too high to police. Use the Customer-approved AI tools, which are designed to handle code without training-data leakage.

sections.heading: 'Will productivity gains accrue to us as the vendor or to the Customer?'
paras: Under staff augmentation the Customer captures the gain through reduced hours, increased throughput per squad-month, or scope rebasing. Vendor's value-share comes through scope expansion, longer engagements, and reputation — see §11.

sections.heading: 'What happens if a vendor developer leaves mid-engagement?'
paras: The vendor JML feed (mandatory under the SOW Addendum) triggers identity disablement within 24 hours. Tool entitlement is reclaimed. Replacement personnel onboard via the standard 5-day flow.

sections.heading: 'What if our squad uses a different IDE that doesn't support Copilot Enterprise well?'
paras: Discuss with the Customer DevEx team. The supported IDE list is reviewed quarterly; reasonable additions are accommodated. The Customer-approved tooling stack is the baseline; the IDE is negotiable.

sections.heading: 'Can our developers use AI to write tests, even if they don't use it for production code?'
paras: Yes — and it is encouraged. AI-generated tests still go through PR review and must be meaningful (not coverage padding).

sections.heading: 'Does the AUP apply to subcontractors we use?'
paras: Yes. The SOW Addendum requires flow-down. The Customer holds the vendor accountable for subcontractor compliance and may require named individuals to attest individually.

sections.heading: 1. Executive Summary
paras: Group Fintech runs release cycles across 17 markets supporting 290M+ customers. Quality assurance is currently squad-embedded, manual-heavy, and uneven in coverage. This strategy establishes an AI-driven test automation capability that will lift regression coverage by 3×, reduce release cycle time by 35%, and cut production defect escape rates by half within 12 months.

The approach is pragmatic: start with two pilot squads, prove measurable value in 90 days, then scale across engineering. We build on commercial LLMs for test generation, open-source frameworks for execution, and lightweight ML for defect-risk prediction — no vendor lock-in, no moonshot bets.
Headline targets (12 months):
Regression coverage: baseline → 3× across pilot squads
Release cycle time: −35%
Production defect escape rate: −50%
Flaky test rate: −60%
Engineer hours reclaimed from manual test maintenance: ~25% per pilot squad

sections.heading: 2. Problem Statement
paras: Across Group Fintech engineering, testing is the primary bottleneck slowing release confidence. The pattern is consistent across squads:
Regression suites grow faster than they are maintained — flakiness compounds, teams disable failing tests rather than fix them
Test generation is still manual and driven by developer discretion, leading to uneven coverage of edge cases and non-happy-path flows
Defect prediction is reactive — issues are discovered in staging or production rather than prevented at PR time
Cross-squad test patterns and fixtures are not shared, each squad reinvents its tooling
QA engineers spend an outsized share of their time on maintenance rather than strategic coverage design
The cost of this is not primarily test infrastructure — it is slower releases, deferred feature work, and a compliance tax every time a significant wallet change ships.

sections.heading: 3.1 Primary Objectives
paras: Establish an AI-assisted test automation capability as a division-wide shared service within 6 months
Prove measurable release confidence uplift in two pilot squads within 90 days of capability launch
Scale to five additional squads by end of Q4 2026 with self-service tooling and playbooks
Publish internal standards for AI-generated test code review, security, and maintainability

sections.heading: 3.2 Secondary Objectives
paras: Feed anonymised test outcomes into the broader AI platform to improve defect prediction over time
Reduce the total QA headcount pressure per squad by shifting maintenance load to the shared service
Create a defensible capability the Group Risk & Compliance function can audit for regulated releases

sections.heading: 4.1 In Scope
paras: Unit, integration, API, and end-to-end UI test generation and maintenance
CI/CD pipeline integration at the PR and merge-to-main stages
Defect-risk scoring on PRs (recommend reviewers, flag high-risk changes)
Self-healing selectors for UI tests
Flaky test detection and auto-quarantine
Test data management for pilot squads

sections.heading: 4.2 Out of Scope (Phase 1)
paras: Performance and load testing (deferred to Phase 2)
Security penetration testing (handled by Security Testing function)
Mobile device farm management (separate investment)
Manual exploratory testing — remains a human-led activity and will not be replaced

sections.heading: 5.2 Build vs. Buy
paras: The vendor scan (Diffblue, Mabl, CodiumAI, Testim) shows strong point solutions but none cover the full pipeline we need at the Group's scale and compliance bar. The decision is to build a thin internal layer on commercial LLMs and open-source execution frameworks, avoiding lock-in and preserving the ability to switch model providers.

sections.heading: 5.3 Human-in-the-Loop Design
paras: All AI-generated test code lands as a PR authored by the test-generation agent. A human engineer reviews and approves before merge. The agent does not merge its own code. This is deliberate — we are augmenting engineering judgement, not replacing it.
